title: Shortest Word Distance
statement:
You are given a list of words `wordsDict` and two different strings `word1` and `word2`. Both strings occur in `wordsDict`, each possibly more than once. The distance between two positions of the list is the absolute difference of their indices.

Return the smallest distance between a position that holds `word1` and a position that holds `word2`.
constraints: wordsDict[i] consists of lowercase English letters
word1 and word2 both occur in wordsDict
signature: int shortestDistance(String[] wordsDict, String word1, String word2)
notes:
## Intuition

The direct idea is to list every index of `word1`, every index of `word2`, and try all pairs, which costs O(a·b). But for any position of one word, the best partner of the other word is the nearest one, and when scanning left to right, the nearest earlier partner is simply the **last** one seen. So two pointers that only move forward, each remembering the latest index of its word, are enough to see every pair that could be the answer.

## Approach

1. Set `index1` and `index2` to `-1` (not seen yet) and `best` to `wordsDict.length`, larger than any real distance.
2. Walk `i` over the list. If the word is `word1`, move `index1` to `i`; if it is `word2`, move `index2` to `i`.
3. Once both have been seen, `Math.abs(index1 - index2)` is the distance of the closest pair ending at this step; keep the minimum in `best`.
4. Return `best` after the scan.

## Example 1, step by step

`wordsDict = ["practice", "makes", "perfect", "coding", "makes"]`, `word1 = "coding"`, `word2 = "practice"`.

- `i = 0`: `"practice"` sets `index2 = 0`; `index1` is still `-1`, so no distance yet.
- `i = 1, 2`: other words, nothing changes.
- `i = 3`: `"coding"` sets `index1 = 3`. Both are known, so `best = min(5, |3 - 0|) = 3`.
- `i = 4`: `"makes"`, the distance is still 3.

The answer is `3`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n · L): one pass over the `n` words, each comparison costing at most the word length `L` (at most 10).
- Space: O(1): only two indices and the best distance.

## Pitfalls

- Do not stop at the first pair found: in `["a", "y", "y", "y", "b", "y", "y", "a", "b"]` the closest pair is the last one.
- Compare whole words with `===`; `"ab"` and `"abc"` must not match each other.
- Only measure once **both** indices are set, or `-1` produces a fake small distance.
- The pair can appear in either order, so take the absolute difference.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `index1` | latest index of `word1`, or `-1` |
| `index2` | latest index of `word2`, or `-1` |
| `best` | smallest distance found so far |
| `i`, `word` | the current position and its word |

narration.2: index1 will point at the latest word1 seen; -1 means none yet.
narration.3: index2 does the same for word2.
narration.4: Start best above any real distance, which is at most length - 1.
narration.6: Scan the list once from left to right; both pointers only move forward.
narration.7: Read the word at the current position.
narration.8: Is this an occurrence of word1?
narration.9: Move the word1 pointer here: it is now the nearest word1 for anything to the right.
narration.11: Is this an occurrence of word2?
narration.14: A distance only exists once both words have been seen.
narration.15: The two latest positions form the closest pair ending here; keep the smaller distance.
narration.18: Every candidate pair was measured; return the smallest distance.
